documents.abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that viewers tend to evaluate AI-generated advertisements negatively. We argue that viewers can nevertheless enjoy creative advertisements produced by AI. However, the belief that creativity is an exclusively human attribute may prompt cognitive regulation when AI involvement is disclosed. Using a consumer neuroscience approach, we conducted a one-factor, three-level between-subjects experiment in which participants viewed advertisements with no disclosure, disclosure of human–AI collaboration, or disclosure of full AI creation. Creative advertisements elicited joy, captured by facial expression analysis, regardless of whether they were created by humans or AI. Greater joy was associated with less message counterarguing and more favourable advertisement attitudes, but only in the absence of AI disclosure. These findings suggest that AI disclosure does not diminish initial enjoyment. Instead, it may act as a persuasion knowledge cue that activates cognitive regulation, leading viewers to override their positive affective responses when subsequently evaluating the advertisement.

Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now employed in many visual design programs to create images rapidly, but these images may not meet the designer's expectations at first glance. This paper studies mismatch via text prompting, parameters and presets, reference-based input, and in-canvas manipulation. The fourteen academic sources in the review include thirteen peer-reviewed publications from 2024-2026 and Shneiderman's original work on direct manipulation. The workflow stage, participant group, interaction pattern, and the five dimensions of efficiency, perceived control, cognitive load, creative agency, and output predictability were used for evidence coding. Based on this evidence, the demand for refinement reduces the apparent advantage of rapid exploration. Effort saved in generation may be recovered by reducing prompt modifications, filtering output, or re-retrieving a suitable image. More local interactions help express and observe the decisions, but they do not eliminate the uncertainty in the generated results. Evidence for the parameters and presets is relatively scarce, so all four patterns cannot be evaluated equally. This framing clarifies how interface design, rather than model capability alone, affects professional agency and supports more informed tool selection in creative practice.

Open Educational Resources (OER) in higher education are shifting from models centred on the creation and storage of learning materials towards structures characterised by greater connectivity and institutionalisation. This study analyses this development across four dimensions: the emergence of repositories; infrastructure connectivity and interoperability; the institutionalisation of OER in association with Open Educational Practices (OEP); and the formation of adaptive OER ecosystems. Drawing on a review and mapping of the literature, policy analysis, and a comparison of selected prominent OER initiatives, the study conceptualises the development of OER as a five-level progression: repository, organised production, institutionalisation, ecosystem, and adaptive/AI-enabled ecosystem. The findings indicate that repositories constitute a necessary infrastructural condition, but are insufficient in themselves to ensure the effective use, reuse, and sustainability of OER. Interoperability, stakeholder capacities, pedagogical practices, policies, and governance mechanisms become increasingly important as OER expands. Accordingly, the study argues that an OER ecosystem should be understood as a structure comprising interconnected components that can adapt to technological change, particularly the development of generative AI.

The revised United States guidance on model risk management, issued in April 2026, applies its principles to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models, and places generative and agentic AI explicitly outside its scope. This survey follows the models used against fraud and financial crime across that line, from rules, scorecards, and statistical tests, through non-generative machine learning, to generative models and language-model agents, across six fraud types. Unlike prior surveys, we place all three generations in one decision-theoretic frame: we restate in one notation known results on cost-optimal and capacity-constrained alerting, undersampling calibration, and the identifiability of recall from alert feedback, express each generation's model, explanation, and validation quantity in that frame, and add two stylized models, one showing why mean aggregation dilutes the neighborhood signal of camouflaged fraudsters and one showing how verifier independence bounds the residual errors in a generated narrative. We find that statistical models and non-generative machine learning have mature validation practice anchored in supervisory guidance, that generative AI now appears both as a tool of fraudsters and as a component of defenses, and that in hybrid pipelines the generative component can write what an analyst or examiner reads although no dedicated supervisory framework covers it. We therefore formalize the evidence-traceability controls that can supply this missing validation as a division of verification labor, between the drafting agent, a deterministic field check, an independent verifier and the human examiner, governed by three parameters an institution can estimate; we then compare the generations quantity by quantity and close with a research agenda.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study comparatively examines the communication environments and practices of Generations Z, Alpha, and Beta within the framework of media ecology. Generations are treated not as biological age cohorts but as experiential and epistemic regimes shaped by the dominant communication medium. The study is not an empirical field investigation but offers a conceptual and typological comparison. It draws on established empirical literature for Generation Z, platform and interface studies along with child and media research for Generation Alpha, and critical discourse analysis of technology vision texts and the sociotechnical imaginaries approach for Generation Beta. The comparison proceeds along five parameters namely dominant medium, mode of interaction, content production model, epistemic authority, and socio-communicative role. The findings suggest a gradual shift in communication from network-based human-to-human interaction toward human-artificial intelligence interaction and a relocation of epistemic authority from peer groups and algorithmic feeds to personalized artificial intelligence agents. The study argues that this shift necessitates reconsidering the sender-receiver model alongside actor-network theory and the human-machine communication literature.

The increasing use of large language models for code generation calls for methods that distinguish purely human-written code from AI-involved code: files in which any part, however small, was generated or substantially modified by a model. Beyond flagging such files, we aim to localize the lines or blocks attributable to AI. Existing approaches compress a file into a single score, from surface stylistic features or a global code representation, which averages away the evidence when only a few blocks are AI-involved. We propose a framework that models AI authorship at the token level and predicts at the line, block, and file levels. A frozen code language model is equipped with two low-rank adapters, trained separately on machine-written and human-written files; their per-token log-likelihood ratio provides local evidence of AI authorship. Lightweight heads aggregate this evidence within lines and blocks, using the surrounding code context, and their local predictions are aggregated into a file-level decision. We train on mixed-authorship files built from human originals and their AI-generated or AI-modified counterparts, including continuation and fill-in-the-middle scenarios. On an internal test set of 11,773 AI-involved files across six generation regimes against 2,541 human files, our method reaches 72.4 macro F1 at a 1% FPR operating point. With no adaptation, it reaches 62.5 line-level F1 on HybridCodeAuthorship, an external human-AI co-writing benchmark with no training split, above the 56 its own paper reports as the best line-level result. On 19,445 human-written files from repositories created before 2022, the false-positive rate stays between 0.55% and 0.81% under the transported 1% threshold, so the operating point holds on real human code.

This chapter introduces the fundamental principles of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) within the context of Sports Science and data-driven analytics. It demonstrates how unstructured textual and vocal data complement traditional numerical performance metrics by capturing contextual, psychological, and communicative aspects of sport environments. The chapter systematically presents core NLP techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, topic modeling, and word embeddings, and explains their role in transforming language-based data into structured representations for performance analysis and decision-making. Building on these foundations, the chapter examines key neural network architectures used in NLP, particularly recurrent neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory models, and Transformer-based systems. Special emphasis is placed on the attention mechanism and its role in enabling scalable and context-aware language modelling. The chapter further analyzes the capabilities and limitations of Large Language Models, including their generative potential, adaptability through fine-tuning and prompt-based interaction, and challenges such as hallucinations, bias, and interpretability. Through multimodal integration and applied case studies, the chapter highlights how NLP and LLMs contribute to sports analytics, athlete monitoring, talent identification, and real-time decision-making.

Lunar exploration has shifted from single flights to a planned buildup of permanent infrastructure. NASA flew four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II in April 2026, and within eight weeks announced the first three robotic Moon Base missions along with close to a billion dollars in contracts for surface rovers, cargo landers and hopping drones. A parallel programme led by China and Russia, the International Lunar Research Station, is working towards a basic configuration by 2035 with a nuclear power unit delivered between 2033 and 2035. This paper examines the machines that will carry out most of the work in both programmes. It sets out the supervised autonomy model that governs how humans and robots divide decisions under communication delay, identifies the specific artificial intelligence techniques that lunar robots depend on, and proposes an interaction protocol for surface operations. The paper then turns to security. Nearly every capability needed for lunar construction, survey and resource extraction has an obvious military application, and the argument advanced here is that any confrontation on the Moon would be short, machine-led and fought over access to a small number of usable sites rather than over territory in the terrestrial sense. Gaps in the Outer Space Treaty and in the Artemis Accords are assessed against that prospect.

Introduction: Gamification incorporates game design elements into educational activities and offers opportunities to strengthen student participation. However, its effects depend on planning, curricular objectives and implementation conditions. The aim was to analyse its relationship with student motivation and identify opportunities and challenges relevant to Ecuadorian upper secondary education. Methodology: A narrative review of twenty publications on motivational foundations, gamification and learning was developed, incorporating international contributions and a review situated in Ecuador. The synthesis addressed four dimensions: foundations, motivation, pedagogical opportunities and implementation challenges. Published findings were distinguished from teaching guidance derived from their interpretation. Results: The reviewed meta-analyses report favourable, although variable, effects on cognitive, motivational and behavioural outcomes. Evidence specifically concerning intrinsic motivation indicates a small effect, alongside improvements in autonomy and relatedness and a smaller effect on perceived competence. Feedback, progressive challenges and collaboration offer pedagogical possibilities, whereas controlling rewards, exclusionary competition, access barriers and assessment restricted to points require attention. Conclusions: Gamification can enrich teaching when game elements are linked to verifiable learning and inclusive participation opportunities. Its application to Ecuadorian upper secondary education requires contextual adaptation and assessment of understanding and sustained motivation. The narrative approach and diversity of sources limit generalisation and do not permit attribution of effects to specific institutions or causal conclusions about the Ecuadorian school context.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

Heritage museums balance a dual mission: preserving culture and providing educational experiences. As institutions adopt AI-generated audio guides, narrator acoustic features—such as gender and age—significantly impact visitor experiences. This study examines how AI narrator gender and age influence Korean-English bilingual youths’ (ages 15–24) perceptions across two domains: the cultural function (belonging and empathy) and the educational function (comprehensibility and professionalism). Utilizing a between-subjects design, 71 participants were randomly assigned to one of four AI voice conditions (young/old, female/male) to evaluate audio guides for two heritage sites (Korea’s Geunjeongjeon and France’s Hall of Mirrors). A two-way ANOVA revealed older voices yielded significantly higher scores across both functions. For the educational function, male voices independently scored higher than females. For the cultural function, a significant interaction emerged, with older male voices scoring highest. These findings demonstrate that AI voices are not merely neutral information-delivery tools, but active social cues that shape cultural resonance and credibility. Older voices were associated with higher perceived educational and cultural function ratings, while older male voices received the highest cultural-function rating. Consequently, the study suggests that museums must move beyond default voice settings and strategically align AI personas with specific communicative goals.

This review examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can widen educational opportunity while also reproducing social inequality. An integrative review synthesized 24 sources: 17 Indonesian publications (2022–2026), identified through national journal portals and Google Scholar, and seven international policy documents and scholarly works (2016–2023) selected as conceptual anchors. Thematic analysis produced four themes: unequal access, unequal digital and AI literacy, unequal capacity to benefit from AI-supported learning, and governance risks involving privacy, bias, academic integrity, and human agency. The reported benefits of generative AI, such as tutoring, writing support, and translation, appear to depend on connectivity, devices, language resources, teacher competence, and students' ability to evaluate machine output. The Indonesian evidence is mostly cross-sectional, self-reported, or based on small single-institution samples, with little evidence on learning outcomes. One national household analysis of school participation (not AI use) found no significant difference between 3T (disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost) and matched non-3T households, suggesting that regional labels may be an imperfect proxy for household conditions. The review proposes a cumulative model of AI inequality that extends van Dijk's sequence of digital inequality with a governance stage and a feedback loop. The model is a conceptual proposition, not a tested result, and recommendations are ordered by the strength of supporting evidence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping content production in the cultural and creative industries by shifting cultural material organization, script writing, exhibition interpretation, and cultural tourism communication from linear manual workflows to human-AI collaborative workflows. Focusing on productivity improvement and the boundary of creative labor substitution, this research constructs a three-group comparison framework involving human-only creation, AI-assisted creation, and fully AI-generated creation. Based on public cultural heritage data, cultural policy texts, and cultural tourism communication samples from 2018 to 2024, LLMs, RAG, Sentence-BERT semantic retrieval, expert scoring, and mixed-effects ANOVA are combined to measure generation quality, policy suitability, and substitution intensity across different cultural tasks. The results show that the average completion time of the AI-assisted group decreases from 44.2 min to 25.7 min, while the overall quality score increases from 82.6 to 84.1, indicating that human-AI collaboration can improve production efficiency while maintaining content quality. Although the fully AI-generated group achieves the lowest time cost, its policy suitability and cultural accuracy decline noticeably. Task complexity further affects substitution intensity. Cultural tourism copy and short-video scripts are more substitutable, while exhibition interpretation and policy explanation still rely on human judgment. These findings provide quantitative evidence for AI adoption, creative labor restructuring, and cultural policy governance.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of educational evaluation reform, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) has been increasingly applied to performance assessment, yet its actual effects and challenges remain underexplored. This study surveyed 50 undergraduate students to examine their perceptions of GAI-based performance assessment across five dimensions: evaluation efficiency and feedback timeliness, accuracy and fairness, appropriateness of scoring criteria and weight distribution, stability and trust, and deep learning and innovation. Results show that over 70% of respondents recognized GAI's advantages in scoring speed and feedback timeliness, and most regarded its scoring criteria as clear and consistent. However, nearly 75% believed GAI failed to identify innovative highlights, over 70% perceived a tendency to emphasize form over content, and 44% reported that such preferences constrained their creative expression. Respondents also raised concerns about incorrect information, technical instability, and the lack of emotional interaction compared with human evaluation. These findings suggest that GAI should act as an auxiliary tool rather than a full replacement for teacher evaluation. To address current limitations, it is necessary to improve GAI's deep evaluation and fact-checking capabilities, establish human-machine collaborative review mechanisms, and cultivate students' critical thinking. This study provides implications for integrating GAI into university performance assessment.

Nail art has evolved from a decorative beauty practice into a personalized cosmetic service that reflects individual image, style, and self-expression. Nevertheless, nail color selection remains largely dependent on personal preference, fashion trends, social-media images, and practitioner experience rather than standardized color-harmony criteria. This integrative review examines how objective skin color science, nail art design characteristics, personal color concepts, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be combined to establish a methodological basis for personalized nail color selection. The literature on human skin color measurement, CIELAB colorimetry, color-difference analysis, personal color and nail color matching, virtual beauty technologies, and skin-tone bias in AI-generated imagery was synthesized. The evidence supports representing hand skin color as a multidimensional profile based on L*, a*, b*, chroma, and hue angle rather than relying solely on warm/cool or seasonal categories. Nail art should likewise be described using colorimetric, optical, reflective, decorative, and compositional features. Generative AI offers a scalable means of creating standardized virtual hand–nail stimuli, but current evidence demonstrates substantial skin-tone imbalance and potential color inaccuracy in generated images. We therefore propose a six-stage framework: hand skin-color profiling, nail-art feature classification, generative AI-based virtual image generation, colorimetric accuracy and bias validation, skin–nail harmony modeling, and personalized guideline development. This framework should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as a validated recommendation system. External validation using objectively measured human hand skin color and perceptual evaluation is required before clinical, commercial, or professional implementation.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market, yet it remains unclear whether students’ appraisal of AI-driven employment threat translates into employment anxiety in similar ways across cultural groups. This study administered an online questionnaire to 1,595 domestic students (1,095) and international students (500) enrolled at Central South University. Perceived AI replacement threat, AI optimism, and employment anxiety were assessed with 13 five-point Likert items. Information channels, coping behaviors, desired institutional support, and perceived coping relief were assessed as supplementary measures. Confirmatory factor analyses supported an acceptable three-factor structure in both groups. The distinction between threat and anxiety remained qualified due to their substantial association. Metric invariance was established, and partial scalar invariance was obtained after the intercept of Q21 was freed. Perceived AI replacement threat and employment anxiety remained empirically distinguishable, although their latent correlation was stronger among international students than among domestic students. In the structural model, threat was strongly associated with anxiety ( β = 0.764) and weakly associated with optimism ( β = 0.133). After threat was included, optimism showed a small negative conditional association with anxiety ( β = −0.152). The indirect association through optimism was negative but limited in magnitude, and equivalent cross-sectional specifications fit the data equally well. This pattern is best interpreted as an exploratory statistical finding compatible with suppression, rather than confirmed evidence of a directional psychological mechanism. Supplementary coping analyses were descriptive and exploratory. These findings provide qualified empirical support for a three-factor framework of students’ responses to AI-related employment uncertainty, and highlight differences in threat-anxiety coupling across student populations. The results carry implications for targeted student support services addressing AI-related career concerns.

As generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into education and teaching, the question of how to leverage teachers' professional judgment and achieve effective human-machine collaboration has become a significant issue. Based on the theories of AI-TPACK and SAMR, this study focuses on the human-machine co-creation mechanism in the design of high school English teaching activities supported by generative AI. The research employs semi-structured interviews and design-based research methods. By interviewing three high school English teachers, their AI-TPACK performance and practical dilemmas are analyzed. Subsequently, a human-machine co-creation teaching operation model is constructed, and two rounds of practice are carried out in a high school English poetry appreciation course. The research findings indicate that teachers have developed a certain awareness of AI integration, yet they still encounter problems such as poor adaptation to students' learning situations, insufficient output evaluation, and inadequate collaboration mechanisms. The practice shows that continuous negotiation, evaluation, and reconstruction under teachers' guidance are the keys to achieving effective human-machine co-creation.

documents.abstract: Abstract Prior studies exploring teachers’ perceptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini have signaled tensions between instructors’ perceptions of GenAI’s usefulness and their beliefs regarding its ethicality. The current study furthers this line of inquiry, examining issues of ethics and utility by focusing specifically on teachers of languages other than English. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, this study employed a survey to understand language instructors’ ( N = 101) perceptions of the ethicality of GenAI tool use in higher education, along with their perceptions of the usefulness of GenAI for supporting second language (L2) learning. Semi-structured interviews were then conducted with six teachers to further understand participants’ survey responses, with some teachers sharing additional artifacts (e.g., course policies regarding GenAI). The findings suggest that most teachers (92.1%) believe GenAI tools are ethical if used for specific purposes. There also appears to be a connection between teachers’ ethical beliefs and their perceptions of GenAI’s utility, in terms of whether GenAI is used by students as a scaffold/support mechanism versus being used to produce content. The implications of this study provide a roadmap for developing discipline-specific guidelines that preserve L2 learning integrity while leveraging GenAI’s utility.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored across health care for clinical decision-making and education. Within digital health, workforce readiness and digital capability are recognized as critical to successful technology implementation. Midwifery faces persistent workforce challenges including limited protected learning time, restricted leadership development opportunities, and unclear career pathways, yet it is unclear whether generative AI has been examined as a tool to support midwifery workforce development. A scoping review was conducted following the framework of Arksey and O’Malley with PRISMA-ScR reporting. EBSCOhost (CINAHL, MEDLINE, ERIC), Google Scholar, and Elicit were searched for English-language studies published between 2015 and 2026 examining AI in midwifery in relation to at least one of the following: post-registration education, workforce, professional development, leadership, and career progression. Findings were synthesized using framework analysis. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Research focused predominantly on clinical decision-making, predictive models, and undergraduate education. No studies examined generative AI tools to support practicing midwives’ professional development, leadership, or career progression. Attitudes towards AI varied with digital literacy, generational cohort, and ethical concerns. Generative AI in midwifery workforce development is unexamined in the empirical literature. Further research is required to understand acceptability, risks, and value within an ethically governed implementation framework.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is reshaping health sciences education. For nursing students, educational interaction (EI), self-regulated learning (SRL), and GAI interaction are all particularly important. However, these relationships and their processes remain underexplored. Methods A total of 1020 nursing students were recruited from one medical university in Hunan Province in China. The Demographics Questionnaire, the Chinese version of Student-GAI interaction scale, the Educational Interaction Scale, and the Self-regulated Learning Questionnaire were administered. SPSS 22.0 and AMOS 24.0 software were used to analyze the data. Results The mean scores of student-GAI interaction (SGI) and EI were 14.80 ± 2.27 and 70.90 ± 8.15, respectively. Significant positive relationships were found among all three variables (all P < 0.01). Both SGI (β = 0.256) and SRL (β = 0.520) positively were associated with EI (both P < 0.001). Furthermore, SGI showed a significant direct association with EI, with a direct effect value of 0.92 ( P < 0.001). SRL statistically mediated the association between SGI and EI, with a significant indirect effect value of 0.44. The mediating effect represented 32.35% of the total effect ( P < 0.001). Dimension-specific analyses revealed that the mediating effect was strongest for student-teacher interaction (45.41%) and student-content interaction (41.54%). Conclusions SGI is positively associated with EI among nursing students, both directly and indirectly through SRL. Educational strategies that encourage effective GAI use and strengthen SRL may be associated with enhanced EI in nursing education.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the governance of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science academia, emphasizing the intersection of regulatory frameworks, educational practice, and academic integrity. It argues that AI governance in sport must extend beyond general data protection and transparency concerns to address domain-specific risks related to athlete welfare, informed consent, and high-stakes decision-making. The chapter presents a comparative analysis of global regulatory models, including the European Union’s risk-based approach, the United States’ soft-law framework, and diverse Asian and South American strategies, highlighting their implications for academic research and data governance in sport contexts. Further, the chapter explores the integration of AI governance into academic publishing and higher education, outlining converging principles such as human accountability, mandatory disclosure of AI use, and the prohibition of AI authorship. It introduces a harmonic model of AI integration based on active use, critical supervision, and epistemic accountability, positioning AI as a supportive but inherently fallible tool. The chapter also conceptualizes AI literacy as a core competence in sports science education and proposes a structured curriculum governance framework that integrates ethical reasoning, uncertainty interpretation, and responsible AI use. Collectively, the chapter provides a comprehensive foundation for aligning technological innovation with regulatory compliance, educational transformation, and the preservation of scientific integrity in Sports Science.

documents.abstract: Training LLM agents for policy-constrained tool environments, such as an airline backend with booking, refund, and cancellation policies, requires tasks that exercise the environment's rules individually and in combination. Existing synthesis pipelines let a model propose tasks and retain only those it immediately solves, biasing training data toward easier behaviors. We introduce Gradus (Graded Rungs of Ascending Difficulty from an Underlying System), which decouples what a task should teach from the concrete task and solution used to teach it. Without seed tasks, Gradus treats a fixed environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators that capture how actions depend on current conditions and how their effects reshape subsequent decisions. It composes these operators into increasingly demanding tasks while using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations. Crucially, Gradus jointly calibrates tasks and solutions against the environment: execution feedback identifies which side to refine while preserving the intended behavioral requirements. Verification thus becomes a recovery signal rather than a terminal filter, coupling coverage-guided exploration with the preservation of difficult examples. From off-the-shelf backbones, the resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model from 59% to 89% on $τ^2$-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer, and to 76% and 62%, respectively, with an open-weight Qwen3-235B proposer. These results show the value of jointly controlling which behaviors are explored and which survive into verified training data.

The project defines a test environment inspired by the time-loop mechanism featured in the film Groundhog Day. An agent attempts to complete a task; if it makes an error classified as fatal (or exhausts its step budget), the environment is restored to a previously saved checkpoint, while the agent retains a complete, structured memory of all previous loops: the loop counter, cumulative time, summaries of failed attempts, and its own hypotheses. Unlike a conventional episode reset in reinforcement learning (RL), failure information is not lost—it becomes a persistent part of the agent's observations. Additionally, after a reset, the environment may slightly mutate the task conditions, but only when necessary to force the agent to change its strategy (the minimal-intervention principle). These mutations are observable to the agent but are never explicitly signaled. Project objectives: - C1. Build a measurable benchmark for agents' ability to perform within-episode meta-learning (in-context adaptation across resets): the agent should learn from failures without updating its weights. - C2. Investigate whether explicit loop memory reduces time to success compared with an agent without memory (control-group experiments). - C3. Investigate whether minimal changes to task conditions disrupt strategy lock-in, i.e., a situation in which an agent repeatedly attempts variations of the same flawed strategy despite having complete memory of its failures. - C4. Provide a reproducible, deterministic (seeded) harness for experiments with RL agents and LLM-based agents, using a single, unified evaluation protocol. - C5. Identify and measure undesirable emergent behaviors: reward hacking through deliberately triggering resets, learned helplessness, and overfitting to the mutation pattern. Out of scope: gradient-based weight training across loops (the project evaluates in-context adaptation through memory, not through-gradient meta-learning); physical real-time simulation. Artifacts: github.com/casual-art/Groudhog-Day (harness, docs); archive DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23483377.

Aim: This study compared the guideline adherence, clinical safety, risk stratification, source accuracy, and practical applicability of three commercial large language models in perioperative GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) and dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor agonist (GLP-1/GIP RA) management scenarios.Methods: In this non-interventional scenario-based comparative study, 20 English-language perioperative clinical scenarios were submitted once to ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Gemini Advanced/Google AI Pro. documents.abstract: This article presents the results of a theoretical-conceptual study based on a critical analysis of the relevant philosophical literature. The central concepts were traced across the philosophical literature and, on the basis of that analysis, ethical prolepsis is proposed as an attitude of the operative subject toward the foreseeable consequences of their actions, an attitude grounded in accumulated experience and constitutively practical in its orientation, that is, always referred to effective courses of action rather than to formal principles detached from praxis. It is found that, although the anticipatory disposition can be identified at various points in the Western philosophical tradition, it has in no case received a formulation that situates it as an ethical attitude of primary standing, and it is precisely that omission which this work aims to help redress. As part of the proposal, the manifestations of the proleptic attitude are established at the individual and social levels, and its specific relevance to the phenomenon of artificial intelligence (AI) is argued, with attention to the problem of anthropomorphization, whose epistemic and moral consequences are briefly examined in relation to epistemic agency, moral agency, responsibility gaps, and biocomputation.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $δ$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $δ$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

This research examines whether heaviness-location congruency, a sensory correspondence between heaviness and spatial position, improves search performance and usability in digital café menus. Two experiments tested this principle using a simplified two-item selection task and a grid-based menu interface. Experiment 2 assessed effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction and included exploratory eye-tracking analyses. The clearest effect emerged in Experiment 2: congruent layouts enabled faster known-target searches than incongruent and realistic control layouts. Accuracy, subjective time, and satisfaction did not differ significantly between the three interface groups. Composite usability scores (SUM) also showed a significant overall group effect, primarily reflecting the efficiency-related measures of reaction time and subjective time. Exploratory eye-tracking results were broadly consistent with the behavioral findings, with the clearest group difference in the on-target fixation ratio. These findings suggest that heaviness-location congruency may facilitate known-target search efficiency in digital menu interfaces, although benefits for other usability dimensions were not established.

Against the backdrop of profound structural shifts within the global art-auction ecosystem, small- and medium-sized auction houses (SMEs) are confronted with multi-faceted sourcing dilemmas. These include the growing scarcity of high-quality uncirculated artworks ("fresh lots"), diminishing returns from traditional sourcing channels, mounting compliance burdens brought by updated cultural relic regulations, and persistent competitive disadvantages against internationally leading auction institutions. Conventional sourcing workflows rely heavily on personal social networks and individual expert experience, leading to fragmented information storage and limited capacity to expand beyond existing client circles. Although existing academic papers have explored AI-driven artwork valuation, research focusing on AI-assisted upstream sourcing procedures for resource-constrained SME auction houses remains underdeveloped. This paper adopts the Gioia-style grounded-theory inductive qualitative methodology, drawing on five semi-structured in-depth interviews with core practitioners from auction institutions located in the Yangtze River Delta region of China. Through three-phase coding procedures, four aggregate theoretical dimensions are extracted: systemic root causes of sourcing difficulties, fundamental transformation of channel operation logic, structural differentiation of collector behaviours and mindsets, as well as the value boundaries and practical obstacles for AI implementation. Based on these empirical findings, this study constructs an embedded five-stage closed-loop human-AI collaborative sourcing scheme. Different from high-cost custom-built technical systems, the proposed solution adopts zero-code off-the-shelf tooling, explicitly positioning artificial intelligence as an information-augmentation instrument rather than a complete substitute for human professional judgment and trust-based interpersonal negotiation. This research enriches existing literature concerning digital transformation within the art market and delivers context-aware, actionable operational suggestions for SME auction practitioners with limited technical and financial budgets.

Introduction This study investigates the relationship between the L2 motivational self-system and attitudes toward AI-enhanced second language (L2) learning, and tests whether intrinsic and extrinsic motivation mediate these relationships among students learning Chinese or English as a foreign language in Thailand, Macau, and Mainland China. Methods Questionnaire data were collected from 361 participants. Correlational analysis, hierarchical regression, and a bootstrapping approach were used to test mediational relations. Results Both the ought-to L2 self and the ideal L2 self were significantly associated with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning, with the ideal L2 self showing the stronger association. In the overall sample, and in the Thai and Mainland Chinese samples analyzed separately, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation statistically fully mediated the association between the ought-to L2 self and attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning. In the Macau sample, extrinsic motivation was more involved than intrinsic motivation in transmitting this effect. For the ideal L2 self, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation only partially mediated the relationship with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning. Discussion Positive attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning are not formed merely through future self-representations; they are also linked to learners’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. By examining the interaction between the L2 motivational self-system and intrinsic and extrinsic motivation across different regions, this study extends L2 motivation research to the area of AI-enhanced language learning.

Multimodal warnings elicit faster response times than unisensory warnings in cockpits. However, how visual and auditory task demands affect the detection of multimodal warnings remains unclear. This study recruited 30 pilots and 30 control participants to complete a warning response task and an aviation visual or auditory task. The race model inequality analysis indicated that the multisensory enhancement effect decreased as the load increased. The analysis of variance indicated an interaction effect among modality, load level, and task type on response times. Results suggested that demanding tasks may affect the detection of multimodal warnings more substantially than that of unisensory warnings within the same modality. The slowing of response times to multimodal warnings may be driven by the more load-sensitive sensory component. The findings were consistent across groups. This study provides practical implications for multimodal warning design and theoretical insights into multimodal processing.

We analyze the transition from mechanical, high-density digital simulations to authentic human-painted oil works driven by conscious intent. We identify specific formal properties within human-painted physical art that operate as mathematical and structural anomalies—features that remain demonstrably uncomputable by algorithmic loops, prompt injections, or parametric neural networks. ─── 1. Introduction: The Mirage of Materiality in "Sovereign Impasto"Krzysztof Numpsa’s technical evolution note for the SurrCube Sovereign Impasto describes a system designed to merge figure and ground into a unified topological surface using simulated relief and directional brush vectors. However, despite advanced multi-scale ridges and chroma compressions, this digital impasto remains an accumulative simulation lacking the non-linear, conscious pressure of a real human hand. 2. The Theoretical Anchor: Chrono-Acoustic Branes and Ontological TensionTo explain the unique signature of human intent, we look to Numpsa’s framework on dark matter/energy, where baryonic matter forms via standing-wave harmonics on a spacetime membrane governed by observer-induced decoherence. By applying the Novikov self-consistency principle, human intent functions as a closed timelike curve: the artist's final masterpiece acts as a future boundary state, drawing their physical brushstrokes through an "Ontological Tension" (\(\Phi _{\mu \nu }\)) rather than step-by-step calculation. 3. The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the context of Arabic translation learning, particularly in how students utilize AI-generated outputs as considerations in making translation decisions. This study examines Human-AI Collaboration (HAC) among students of the Arabic Language Education Study Program at Universitas Negeri Makassar, focusing on patterns of student interaction with AI-based technologies during the translation process, the distinction between critical and passive use, the competencies that students report developing, the risks that arise, and the factors influencing their use of AI. The study employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through observation, semi-structured in-depth interviews, and documentation involving students and lecturers with experience in teaching the Tarjamah course. The data were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, supported by coding of students’ actions and decisions throughout the translation process. The findings indicate that HAC can be considered critical when students do not merely request translations from AI but also examine, compare, evaluate, revise, or reject AI suggestions before making translation decisions. In contrast, passive use is characterized by limited verification and the direct acceptance or copying of AI-generated outputs. Critical interaction was associated with students’ reported development of linguistic awareness, digital literacy, and evaluative practices, whereas passive use posed a risk of unnoticed semantic and pragmatic errors. AI was also perceived as having limitations when used to translate expressions closely associated with cultural, literary, and religious contexts. Based on the findings of the case study, this study formulates a conceptual framework of Human-AI Collaboration for Arabic translation learning comprising AI-assisted consultation, student verification and evaluation, revision, and student decision-making, with lecturer guidance and prior academic habits serving as contextual factors. This framework is formulated on the basis of the case study findings and is not presented as a learning model that has been validated or experimentally tested.

The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human cognitive activities and creating a growing need to preserve cognitive autonomy in human–AI interactions. Although recent research has examined metacognition in AI-mediated environments, existing work has primarily focused on improving AI use and human–AI collaboration, with less attention to how individuals regulate the role and extent of AI involvement in their own cognitive activities. To address this gap, the present study introduced Human-Centered AI Metacognition (HC-AIM), defined as the capacity to recognize AI capabilities and limitations, monitor AI-generated information, and regulate the extent to which AI participates in one’s own cognitive activities while maintaining cognitive autonomy. Across three studies, we developed the Chinese version of the Human-Centered AI Metacognition Scale (HC-AIMS) and conducted an initial psychometric evaluation. Study 1 examined the scale structure using exploratory factor analysis and supported a predominantly unidimensional structure with good internal consistency. Study 2 examined this structure using confirmatory factor analysis and provided evidence of its convergent validity through its association with general metacognition. Study 3 further replicated the scale structure and internal consistency and examined its relationships with AI literacy, collaborative AI metacognition, and autonomous cognitive offloading. HC-AIM was positively associated with all three constructs. Comparisons of theoretically specified factor models provided preliminary evidence of empirical distinguishability between HC-AIM and both AI literacy and collaborative AI metacognition, despite substantial correlations with these constructs. HC-AIM was also positively associated with autonomous cognitive offloading, providing complementary self-reported criterion-related evidence for its validity. Taken together, the findings suggest that HC-AIM represents a contextualized, human-centered form of metacognitive regulation that is closely related to broader metacognitive and AI-related competencies while specifically emphasizing the regulation of AI participation in human cognition. The Chinese version of the HC-AIMS provides a theoretically grounded starting point for investigating human cognition and cognitive autonomy in AI-mediated environments.

Open-ended Student Evaluations of Teaching (SET) provide rich information about students’ learning experiences and instructional needs, yet their large-scale analysis remains difficult to conduct through manual coding alone. This study proposes a human-in-the-loop artificial intelligence framework for transforming open-ended student feedback into structured and interpretable evidence for educational evaluation. The framework integrates manual thematic coding, natural language processing, generative AI-supported interpretation, and human expert review. Its analytical and interpretive components were evaluated using 344 comment units collected from 43 university students across four open-ended questions administered at two points during a 16-week AI-assisted blended English as a Foreign Language course. TF-IDF with k-means, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and BERTopic were benchmarked in terms of topic coherence, topic distinctiveness, and interpretability. LDA achieved the highest coherence score (0.4224), whereas BERTopic demonstrated the highest topic distinctiveness (IRBO = 0.9889). After hyperparameter optimisation, LDA coherence increased from 0.4224 to 0.4785. The optimised topics were subsequently interpreted using generative AI and examined against manually derived themes, showing broad semantic correspondence across language skills, cognitive processes, affective factors, motivational factors, learning strategies, classroom environments, and educational technologies. The findings indicate that human-in-the-loop AI can improve the scalability and interpretability of qualitative educational feedback while retaining human oversight of contextual judgement. By combining computational analysis with generative AI-supported interpretation and expert review, the proposed framework provides a practical analytical basis for evidence-informed educational feedback and subsequent instructional decision-making.

documents.abstract: How can we effectively oversee AI systems that surpass human intelligence? AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing positions and a judge, either a human or a weaker model, decides which is correct. By facilitating supervisors in providing high-quality training signals, debate aims to encourage truthful and safe behavior from AI systems whose capabilities exceed our own. However, human judgment is not neutral: people often rely on biases which advanced AI systems may learn to exploit. Drawing on insights from collective intelligence and social cognition, this paper investigates whether debate can guide human and LLM supervisors toward the truth despite their prior beliefs. We evaluate several protocol configurations. We also explore setups inspired by the wisdom of the crowd such as the number and diversity of judges, as well as interaction mechanisms including deliberation and voting. Overall, we find that debate increases accuracy relative to prior beliefs for human judges, whereas the consultancy baseline, in which a single expert argues for one answer, does not. For weaker language models, however, the results are mixed: debate provides no comparable gains in most settings and can even reduce accuracy. Among multi-judge protocols, weighted voting produces the highest accuracy for human supervisors, whereas for LLMs none of them significantly improves group accuracy, even as the number of judges increases. Notably, the behavior of minority judges in non-diverse deliberation protocols suggests that, under symmetric settings, incorrect positions could be more persuasive than correct ones. These findings support debate as a viable path toward scalable human oversight, but cast doubt on its benefits for weaker AI supervisors, raising concerns about fully automated training and control pipelines in high-stakes settings.

documents.abstract: Momentum is central to stochastic optimization in deep learning, including the training of large language models. Classical momentum methods typically rely on a fast exponential moving average (EMA) scheme, which discounts past gradients on a fixed timescale and may underweight older gradients that remain informative. This creates a trade-off between retaining long-term history and adapting to recent changes. We introduce Hybrid Momentum (HyM), which combines a linearly weighted average of past gradients with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The former assigns weights proportional to the gradients' iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the latter emphasizes recent gradients. This hybrid construction is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, we propose HyMUON, which applies Newton--Schulz orthogonalization to the hybrid direction. Illustrative examples and controlled experiments demonstrate the benefits of combining gradient information across these two timescales. Across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling, HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon strong baselines. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14, and in both the 100k- and 600k-step GPT-2 124M OpenWebText regimes. For LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4, HyMUON achieves a final validation loss of 2.777, compared with 2.903 for Muon.

Electrocardiography (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac diagnosis, yet most machine learning methods for ECG analysis lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. We present IECG, a weakly-supervised ECG foundation model that jointly performs diagnostic classification and abnormality localization without requiring manual abnormal region annotations, overcoming a long-standing bottleneck in interpretable ECG learning. Central to IECG is a weakly-supervised attention strategy that explicitly incorporates clinical priors by deriving abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established ECG clinical knowledge. These pseudo-labels guide the model's CLS-token attention through a KL-divergence loss, encouraging it to focus on diagnostically relevant waveform regions. During pretraining, IECG is jointly optimized with clinically guided attention supervision, ECG-text contrastive alignment, and report captioning objectives, enabling it to learn rich multimodal representations while producing localized waveform evidence. By explicitly aggregating features from clinically guided attention regions, IECG grounds its diagnostic predictions in interpretable waveform evidence without sacrificing classification performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IECG achieves state-of-the-art abnormal region localization while maintaining strong classification performance, advancing trustworthy foundation models for ECG analysis.

When Webb, Holyoak, and Lu reported that large language models (LLMs) solve a wide range of analogy problems zero-shot, they reopened an old philosophical question: do such systems reason relationally, or do they exploit surface regularities absorbed from training? Critics show that performance degrades on counterfactual variants that leave human performance intact; defenders answer that these failures reflect peripheral deficits. I argue that the debate lacks a principled criterion for distinguishing genuine relational reasoning from associative pattern-completion, and that Spinoza’s epistemology supplies one. Spinoza separates imagination—general ideas formed through the contingent order in which the body is affected—from reason, the adequate cognition of what is genuinely common through common notions; his own illustration (Ethics 2p40s2) is a proportional analogy that turns on the difference between applying a learned rule and grasping a common form. Reconstructed functionally, the distinction yields a diagnostic heuristic: invariance of competence under transformations that preserve relational structure while destroying surface similarity counts as defeasible evidence of relational grounding. This separates the following two questions the literature conflates: whether a system produces correct analogies, and whether its competence is relationally grounded. I give the criterion a measurement protocol and apply it symmetrically to humans and machines.

The present study aimed to examine differences in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Emotional Intelligence (EI) between adolescents and adults, investigate gender differences, and explore the relationship between AI and EI. The study included 120 participants, comprising 60 adolescents and 60 adults. Data were analysed using the t-test and Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient. The findings revealed no statistically significant differences between adolescents and adults in Artificial Intelligence (t = 0.38) or Emotional Intelligence (t = 0.93) at the 0.05 significance level. Similarly, no significant gender differences were observed in Emotional Intelligence (t = 0.39) or Artificial Intelligence (t = 1.70). Furthermore, the correlation analysis indicated a negligible negative relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Emotional Intelligence (r = −0.056, p = 0.543), which was statistically insignificant. These findings suggest that the studied groups exhibited broadly similar scores across the examined variables, with no significant association between AI and EI. The study highlights the importance of understanding the psychological implications of increasing AI use among different age groups and genders. Further research with larger and more diverse samples is recommended to explore the complex relationship between technological engagement and emotional functioning.

BACKGROUND: World Trade Center (WTC)-exposed Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) rescue/recovery workers have an elevated risk of smoking-related morbidity. Despite access to free tobacco cessation treatment, some individuals in this population continue to smoke. In other settings, opt-out treatment approaches increase treatment initiation, but effectiveness in occupational health programs is unclear. Accordingly, we (1) assessed whether an opt-out strategy increases engagement with a Tobacco Cessation Program and (2) identified factors associated with engagement. METHODS: This was a randomized trial among FDNY firefighters and Emergency Medical Service (EMS) who self-reported smoking and were eligible for the WTC Health Program Lung Cancer Screening Program. 1:1 randomization occurred prior to contact for opt-out recruitment with Enhanced Care treatment (Opt-Out/Enhanced) or opt-in recruitment with Standard Care treatment (Opt-In/Standard). Opt-Out/Enhanced included proactive outreach and tailored biofeedback during counseling; Opt-In/Standard included participant-initiated engagement and standard counseling. Both groups were offered identical no-cost pharmacotherapy (varenicline). Engagement was defined as: consented enrollment (expressed interest and provided informed consent) and treatment initiation (attendance at ≥1 counseling session). Engagement differences were evaluated using logistic regression; sociodemographic and health-related factors were characterized descriptively without formal testing due to small numbers. RESULTS: Overall, 312 individuals were randomized (Opt-Out/Enhanced, n = 156 and Opt-In/Standard, n = 156). Engagement was low (7.4%). Consented enrollment (n = 23; OR = 3.05; 95% CI = 1.11-9.72) and treatment initiation (n = 18; OR = 2.08; 95% CI = 0.72-6.73) were higher in Opt-Out/Enhanced versus Opt-In/Standard. Treatment initiators had a median age of 60.5 (vs 65.0 years among non-initiators); 38.9% were EMS (vs 18.0%), 22.2% were female (vs 6.9%), 77.8% had a prior cessation attempt (vs 23.5%), and 55.6% had abnormal lung function (vs 32.9%). Participants were too few to analyze cessation outcomes in depth. CONCLUSIONS: Despite low engagement overall, opt-out treatment had higher engagement with tobacco cessation treatment. This supports other work that has found opt-out treatment to be encouraged for hard-to-reach populations.

This study examines the technology-integrated instructions’ impact on tertiary students’ behavioural engagement during the task execution. Two main theoretical models were used to explore the independent variable - teachers’ technology integration and the dependent variable ‘behavioural engagement’ during the learning activity. The first construct, pedagogical integration, is premised upon the SAMR model, while the second construct is based on the Fredricks, Blumenfeld, and Paris (2004) three - dimensional engagement model - behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement. The study sampled 535 Arabic-speaking English language learners from arts and science backgrounds enrolled in the Foundation Year programme at a public university in Saudi Arabia. A self-developed questionnaire consisting of 32 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale measured both constructs. The findings show that the statistical assumptions necessary for the analysis were met, allowing for reliable modeling. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) revealed that technology engagement (TE) is best measured as a unidimensional construct, while the pedagogical use of technology (PUT) is multidimensional. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) confirmed a one-factor model for TE and a four-factor model for PUT, with the second-order PUT model providing the best fit. Additionally, the findings highlighted that strategic technology integration by instructors enhances learner engagement even in challenging conditions such as fatigue. Keywords: Pedagogy; Technology; Behaviour; Cognition; Engagement

This study examined the implementation of ChatGPT-assisted Problem-Based Learning (PBL) with a Deep Learning approach in global warming instruction and analyzed changes in students’ scientific literacy before and after the intervention. A pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was used with 30 students in Class X-1 at SMA Negeri 5 Kota Serang during the 2025/2026 academic year. The research instruments consisted of instructional materials, a 22-item scientific literacy test that had passed content and empirical validation, and an observation sheet. Descriptive statistics and a paired-sample t-test were used to analyze the test data, while observation data were summarized as percentages across scientific knowledge, context, science competencies, and science identity. The mean scientific literacy score increased from 76.36 on the pretest to 85.60 on the posttest, and the paired-sample t-test showed a statistically significant difference, t(29) = -6.925, p < .001. Observation results also showed higher percentages in all four scientific literacy aspects during the second learning session. These findings indicate positive changes in students’ scientific literacy following the intervention; however, because the study did not include a comparison group, the changes cannot be attributed exclusively to the intervention.

This chapter operationalizes the concept of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science by translating ethical principles into concrete technical, organizational, and governance requirements for high-risk sporting contexts. It identifies seven core dimensions of trustworthy AI—human agency and oversight, technical robustness, privacy and data governance, transparency, fairness, societal well-being, and accountability—and examines their specific implications for sport environments characterized by physical risk, power asymmetries, and career-defining decisions. The chapter further explores potential risks arising from the misuse or incomplete implementation of these principles, including athlete surveillance, hidden algorithmic decision-making, and deterministic scoring systems that may negatively influence career trajectories. In response, it introduces the Fair Play AI Framework, a sport-specific governance model structured around the PLAY acronym: Procedural Fairness, Lifecycle Autonomy, Authority and Accountability, and Yield to Context. This framework integrates explainability, contestability, contextual validation, and human oversight into a coherent decision-support architecture. By linking ethical theory, regulatory considerations, and applied sport practice, the chapter provides a structured approach for implementing responsible AI systems that enhance performance and health outcomes while preserving athlete autonomy, fairness, and institutional accountability in Sports Science.

documents.abstract: This community service program was conducted to improve teachers' competence in designing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted learning media at Yayasan Rahmat Islamiyah, Medan. The program was motivated by the gap between the rapid development of AI-based educational technology and the limited digital pedagogical capacity of teachers in many Islamic educational foundations, which still rely on conventional, text-based teaching media. Teachers at the foundation faced difficulties in producing communicative visual, audio-visual, presentation, and video-based learning media, as well as in building effective communication with young learners. The program was carried out through four stages adapted from the management cycle of planning, organizing, actuating, and controlling, followed by an evaluation stage using Kirkpatrick's four-level model. Activities included lectures, hands-on workshops, mentoring, and simulation of AI tool usage such as Canva AI, CapCut AI, and presentation-generation platforms, grounded in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework. Results show a significant increase in teachers' knowledge and skills, reflected in pre-test and post-test scores, active participation, and the production of AI-assisted teaching media by all participants. Teachers also reported improved confidence in communicating with children through more engaging, visualized instructional content. This PKM concludes that structured, AI-based media-design training effectively strengthens teacher competence and can serve as a sustainable model for continuous professional development in Islamic educational foundations facing similar digital transformation challenges.

With the rapid development of live-streaming e-commerce and artificial intelligence, human and AI live-streaming have become two product information disclosure formats in online retail. From the perspective of product information disclosure, we develop a game-theoretic model of a live-streaming e-commerce supply chain comprising a brand owner and an e-commerce platform. We derive Stackelberg equilibria under the resale mode through backward induction, obtain the optimal retail price and information disclosure level under the agency mode through joint optimization, and then compare disclosure-format and sales-mode preferences. The results show that (1) AI live-streaming does not always achieve a higher information disclosure level. It leads to a higher disclosure level only when consumer trust in AI live-streaming disclosure is high, or when trust is moderate and sensitivity to the information disclosure level is low; otherwise, human live-streaming disclosure achieves a higher disclosure level. (2) Under the resale mode, the brand owner and the e-commerce platform have consistent preferences regarding disclosure formats. Both prefer AI live-streaming when consumer trust in AI disclosure is high, or when trust is low but sensitivity is also low, whereas both prefer human live-streaming when trust is low and sensitivity is high. Under the agency mode, their preferences diverge when consumer trust is low and sensitivity is moderate. (3) Regarding sales modes, the brand owner prefers the agency mode only when the commission rate and consumer sensitivity to information disclosure are both low; otherwise, it prefers the resale mode. These findings provide theoretical and managerial implications for disclosure-format selection and sales-mode decisions in live-streaming e-commerce.
